method: OPEN AND QUOTED, from the 'Diphtheria' chapter of the Australian Immunisation Handbook, retrieved 2026-09-23. Every pass claim is machine re-checkable. LICENCE: Free to read but NOT openly licensed -- health.gov.au states 'all other rights are reserved'. Quoted with attribution on the same footing as the Stroke Foundation, Kidney Health Australia and NHFA/CSANZ sources already in this compendium.

claims.claim: **Children: 5 doses at 2, 4, 6 and 18 months and 4 years**, as **DTPa-containing** vaccine.
claims.source_text: Diphtheria-toxoid vaccine is recommended in a 5-dose schedule at 2, 4, 6 and 18 months, and 4 years of age. Infants and children receive diphtheria toxoid in combination with tetanus toxoid and acellular pertussis, as DTPa (diphtheria-tetanus-acellular pertussis)-containing vaccines.
claims.locator: Australian Government Department of Health, Disability and Ageing, 'Diphtheria', The Australian Immunisation Handbook, at https://immunisationhandbook.health.gov.au/contents/vaccine-preventable-diseases/diphtheria, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Never-vaccinated adolescents and adults: 3 doses at least 4 weeks apart, then boosters at 10 and 20 years.**
claims.source_text: Adolescents and adults who have never had a diphtheria-toxoid vaccine are recommended to receive 3 doses of diphtheria-toxoid vaccine with at least 4 weeks between doses, and booster doses at 10 years and 20 years after the primary course.
claims.locator: Australian Government Department of Health, Disability and Ageing, 'Diphtheria', The Australian Immunisation Handbook, at https://immunisationhandbook.health.gov.au/contents/vaccine-preventable-diseases/diphtheria, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Rare in Australia but still endemic in many developing countries.**
claims.source_text: Diphtheria is rare in Australia but remains endemic in many developing countries.
claims.locator: Australian Government Department of Health, Disability and Ageing, 'Diphtheria', The Australian Immunisation Handbook, at https://immunisationhandbook.health.gov.au/contents/vaccine-preventable-diseases/diphtheria, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: Two presentations: **respiratory or cutaneous.** ⚠️ **Pharyngeal diphtheria forms a greyish or green membrane in the upper respiratory tract**, and was historically the commonest form in unimmunised people.
claims.source_text: Diphtheria infection may lead to two different clinical outcomes: respiratory disease or cutaneous (skin) disease. Almost any mucous membrane can be involved, with pharyngeal diphtheria historically the most common form of the disease in unimmunised people. Pharyngeal diphtheria is characterised by an inflammatory exudate that forms a greyish or green membrane in the upper respiratory tract.
claims.locator: Australian Government Department of Health, Disability and Ageing, 'Diphtheria', The Australian Immunisation Handbook, at https://immunisationhandbook.health.gov.au/contents/vaccine-preventable-diseases/diphtheria, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Confirmed or suspected diphtheria should be notified IMMEDIATELY.** **Contacts usually need vaccination (primary or booster) AND prophylactic antibiotics.**
claims.source_text: notifiable disease in all states and territories in Australia. Confirmed or suspected diphtheria is of considerable public health importance. It should be notified immediately to state or territory public health authorities. Contacts usually need vaccination (either primary or booster, depending on their vaccination status) and appropriate prophylactic antibiotics.
claims.locator: Australian Government Department of Health, Disability and Ageing, 'Diphtheria', The Australian Immunisation Handbook, at https://immunisationhandbook.health.gov.au/contents/vaccine-preventable-diseases/diphtheria, retrieved 2026-09-23
